chunks: A number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad and Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, all from Ali ibn Mahziyar, who said:

I wrote to Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) informing him that Is'haq ibn Ibrahim endowed a property for Hajj, and its mother of child, and what remained from it for the poor; and that Muhammad ibn Ibrahim witnessed me upon himself with wealth to be distributed among our brethren; and that among the Banu Hashim there is one whose right is known, who speaks with our words, who is in need, so do you think I should direct that to them if his way is the way of charity, because the endowment of Is'haq is indeed charity?

So he (peace be upon him) wrote: 'I understood, may Allah have mercy on you, what you mentioned from the bequest of Is'haq ibn Ibrahim, may Allah be pleased with him, and what Muhammad ibn Ibrahim, may Allah be pleased with him, witnessed to you with that, and what you asked about regarding sending some of that to those from the Banu Hashim who have inclination and affection, who are deserving and poor. So send that to them, may Allah have mercy on you. For they, when they become to this scheme, are more deserving of it than others, due to a meaning, if I were to explain it to you, you would know it, if Allah wills.'
ai.seo_question: Can charity funds be directed to needy members of the Banu Hashim according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi elucidates the Shia jurisprudence of waqf distribution, specifically validating the preference for Banu Hashim who are 'muqarrabun' (close to the Imams) and financially needy, provided their alignment with the Imamate is genuine. Imam al-Sadiq (as) affirms that this specific affinity grants them a superior claim over other eligible recipients, reflecting the theological principle of 'qurbah' (proximity) in charitable allocation. The text highlights the scholarly practice of verifying both the financial need and the doctrinal loyalty of beneficiaries when distributing endowment funds.
